QF.id: SIA Case Studies on SAS Standards_2

question.text: While reviewing the Niwas slum-rehabilitation project, Mr. Arjun Desai (SIA on empanelment waitlist) finds that the SE's own community workers collected 75% of the beneficiary survey data. Under SAS-100 and the general SIA framework, what is the MOST appropriate response?

answer.text: Treat SE-collected data as information-of-Responsible-Party, triangulate against independent sources (municipal records, PMAY database, sub-sample re-interviews) and disclose the reliance in the limitations section
Accept the data at face value because Swagruha has implemented the project for 4 years and has domain knowledge
Reject the engagement because self-reported data by the implementing team renders the assessment invalid
Replace all SE data with fresh primary collection, at the SE's cost, before signing the Social Impact Assessment Report

explanation.text: The Logic: Under SAS-100 a reasonable level of assurance requires that evidence be sufficient and appropriate. The SIA can use Responsible-Party-collected data but must corroborate through independent triangulation (a 10-15% SIA re-survey sub-sample, municipal/PMAY cross-check, photographs) and disclose the reliance — exactly how the Swagruha case study handled the over-dependence on Swagruha community workers for comfort. The Trap: Option C is over-reactive — SE data is admissible, not disqualifying. Option B abandons professional scepticism. Option D is disproportionate and commercially unreasonable on a 4.67 Cr engagement. Cross-Exam Context: This mirrors the reliance-on-management-representations logic in III-A (Compliance) and the 'use of work of another expert' concept in audit-oriented material referenced in XV (Research Analyst). Assessor's Pro-Tip: Always document a re-survey sub-sample (usually 10-15% of the SE sample) — it gives you a cheap reliability test and a defensible limitation paragraph in Section II of the Social Impact Assessment Report.
